summary: The candidate is a substantive partial fix: the exact JsonArrayParser and Qwen25Detector character-stream reproducer passes, but Mistral still loses the trailing valid call and final chunks can leave preserved valid calls stranded because finish() does not drain the buffer.

tests.what_was_measured: On the recorded base, reproduced the exact issue outputs: empty JsonArrayParser result and a corrupt merged Qwen25Detector result. On the candidate, both valid calls were preserved with stable indices.
Candidate focused regression suite: 248 passed and 4 subtests passed.
Independent ordering/chunk-boundary checks across JsonArrayParser, Qwen25, Hermes, Llama32, Mistral, and Trinity; demonstrated Mistral failure and end-of-stream buffered-call loss.

gpu_execution.evidence: The affected implementation and candidate changes are pure Python request parsing; no GPU execution is involved in the original reproducer or contract.

remaining_counterexamples: Mistral canonical-array streaming with valid, unknown, valid calls returns only the first valid call and exposes the remainder as normal text, even with one-character chunks.

A final chunk containing a complete unknown call followed by a valid call leaves that valid call buffered after finish() for JsonArrayParser, Qwen25, Hermes, Llama32, and Trinity; Mistral separately flushes/losses the remainder.
Coarse chunks can leave a trailing valid tool's arguments buffered at end-of-stream because the parser processes only one transition per increment and finish() is a no-op.
remaining_limitations: No full model, HTTP serving, GPU, model-architecture, semantic-accuracy, or distributed-workload validation was performed; none is needed to establish the deterministic parser counterexamples.
The prepared environment has one gfx950 GPU, but using it would not validate this CPU-only parser path.
No native rebuild was performed because neither the candidate nor the relevant implementation changes native code.
